arXiv:2611.18494v1 [cs.AI] 13 Nov 2026

ARCHER: From Rationale Imitation to Executable Reasoning in Small Language Models

Dhruv Dixit Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Affiliation: ddixit1@stevens.edu    Khushi Patel Affiliation: Department of Computer ScienceStevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ - 07030, United States Affiliation: kpatel105@stevens.edu    Congcong Xu Affiliation: cxu7@stevens.edu    Min Song Affiliation: msong6@stevens.edu
Abstract

Small language models are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but they remain unreliable on mathematical reasoning tasks that require decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. We introduce ARCHER: Action-trace Reinforcement for Calculator-grounded Hierarchical Executable Reasoning, a two-stage framework for training small language models (SLMs) to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories. In the first stage, ARCHER compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers. This shifts the supervision target from imitating explanatory text to learning a tool-grounded reasoning policy. In the second stage, ARCHER refines this policy through asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning, using grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. Across five standard sub-10B backbones, ARCHER improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on macro-average across benchmark accuracies, including gains of 8.95 points on MATH-500 and 5.33 and 5.34 points on AIME-2024 and AIME-2025. Evaluations on two additional reasoning-specialized 7B backbones further show that executable grounding remains beneficial after reasoning-focused reinforcement learning or distillation. These results demonstrate that executable supervision and reward-guided behavioral refinement provide a general and effective training paradigm for compact mathematical reasoners.

1 Introduction

Small language models (SLMs) are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but remain unreliable on mathematical tasks requiring decomposition, exact computation, and verification. A correct solution must identify relevant quantities, select operations, preserve intermediate results, and produce a well-formed answer. This motivates training SLMs to generate reasoning trajectories that can be executed and checked, rather than merely fluent explanations.

Chain-of-thought prompting established the value of intermediate reasoning (Wei et al., 2022), motivating rationale supervision and reasoning distillation for smaller models (Hsieh et al., 2023; Shridhar et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2023; Ranaldi and Freitas, 2024). Prior work also studies rationale faithfulness (Wang et al., 2023), efficient reasoning transfer (Chen et al., 2025), and small-large model collaboration (Zhao et al., 2025). However, free-form rationales are non-canonical and often mix reasoning decisions with implicit arithmetic. A compact student may therefore imitate the form of a solution without learning which computations must be executed or how their results should guide later steps.

Tool-augmented methods address this problem by externalizing computation. Program-aided approaches separate language reasoning from executable operations (Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), while faithful reasoning methods connect generated explanations to executable derivations (Lyu et al., 2023). Other systems interleave reasoning with tools or APIs (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2024), including calculator-oriented methods for mathematical reasoning (Kadlčík et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024). These approaches demonstrate the value of execution, but tool access alone does not teach a compact model when to invoke a tool, how to construct a valid call, or how to use the returned observation consistently.

Process supervision and reinforcement learning provide complementary mechanisms for improving reasoning behavior. Process-level methods evaluate intermediate steps rather than only final answers (Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), while recent reasoning models use verifiable outcomes and structured reinforcement-learning objectives (Guo et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025). Tool-integrated reinforcement learning further shows that execution feedback can improve interaction policies (Feng et al., 2025). Nevertheless, reward design remains difficult: sparse outcome signals provide weak credit assignment, while process rewards can be brittle, noisy, or misaligned with reasoning-model outputs (Dai et al., 2025; Dontsov et al., 2026).

In this paper, we address the intersection of these three lines of work. Unlike rationale distillation, our framework replaces free-form explanations with typed executable actions. Unlike tool-access methods, it makes calculator calls, runtime observations, verification, and termination part of the supervised trajectory. Unlike outcome-only or flat process-reward optimization, it organizes feedback into priority-ordered reward families that are activated only when relevant.

We propose ARCHER: Action-trace Reinforcement for Calculator-grounded Hierarchical Executable Reasoning, a two-stage framework for training SLMs as executable mathematical reasoning policies. In Stage 1, TRACE (Tool-augmented Reasoning via Action-Compiled Execution) converts legacy chain-of-thought rationales into typed trajectories containing reasoning actions, calculator calls, deterministic observations, verification actions, and final answers. In Stage 2, HiGRA (Hierarchically Gated Reward Aggregation) refines the TRACE policy using priority-ordered, conditionally gated rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. We evaluate ARCHER across seven sub-10B backbones and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Across five standard backbones, ARCHER improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on average and is best or tied-best in all 40 model-benchmark comparisons; it also improves both reasoning-specialized backbones across all eight benchmarks.

Contributions.

ARCHER makes three contributions. First, it formulates SLM mathematical reasoning as executable policy learning, with typed model actions and deterministic external computation. Second, a compiler framework that converts existing rationale datasets into calculator-grounded supervision without requiring manually authored action traces. Third, a reinforcement learning algorithm that introduces priority-ordered and conditionally gated trajectory rewards that jointly optimize correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace compatibility. Together, these 3 contributions unify rationale supervision, tool-augmented execution, and process-aware reinforcement learning within a single framework for accurate and auditable mathematical reasoning.

2 Related Work

Reasoning supervision and distillation.

Chain-of-thought prompting established the value of intermediate reasoning Wei et al. (2022), motivating rationale supervision and stepwise distillation for smaller models Hsieh et al. (2023); Shridhar et al. (2023). Subsequent work improves rationale faithfulness Wang et al. (2023), generative distillation objectives Gu et al. (2023), transfer efficiency Chen et al. (2025), and small-large model collaboration Zhao et al. (2025). ARCHER instead supervises typed executable actions, delegating computation to a deterministic runtime rather than imitating free-form explanations.

Tool-grounded reasoning.

Program-aided methods separate language reasoning from executable computation Gao et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023), while faithful reasoning connects explanations to executable derivations Lyu et al. (2023). General tool-use frameworks interleave reasoning with actions or APIs Yao et al. (2023); Schick et al. (2023), and calculator-centered methods improve mathematical reasoning through explicit computation and tool feedback Kadlčík et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2024). ARCHER makes this interaction the training target itself by compiling legacy rationales into canonical action-observation traces and optimizing their correctness, grounding, and validity.

Process supervision and reinforcement learning.

Process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning rather than final answers alone Lightman et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2024), while verifiable RL objectives induce stronger reasoning behavior Guo et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025). Tool-integrated and stability-focused studies further expose the difficulty of sparse, noisy, or fragmented rewards Feng et al. (2025); Dai et al. (2025). Recent RL-specialized systems include DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), Kimi k1.5 (Team et al., 2025), MiMo-7B-RL, and Falcon-H1R (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025; Falcon LLM Team, 2026). ARCHER complements these text-only reasoners with deterministic execution and differs from flat reward mixtures by using priority-ordered, conditionally gated reward families for correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment.

3 Methodology

The ARCHER framework, illustrated in Figure 1, has two stages. Stage 1, TRACE, compiles legacy chain-of-thought rationales into calculator-grounded action traces and trains the student by supervised fine-tuning. Stage 2, HiGRA, refines the TRACE policy with grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards. TRACE teaches the model the executable action language; HiGRA improves how reliably the model uses that language to solve problems. Working together, ARCHER does not merely expose the model to tools or rationales; it converts rationale supervision into an executable control interface and then optimizes the model over completed, runtime-executed trajectories.

3.1 Overall Reasoning Policy

Each training example is a tuple (x,r,y⋆)(x,r,y^{\star}), where xx is the input problem, rr is a legacy rationale, and y⋆y^{\star} is the gold answer. ARCHER trains a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} that maps xx to an executable trajectory τ\tau and a final answer y^\hat{y}. A trajectory is a sequence of states τ=(s1,…,sT)\tau=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{T}) and st=(at,ut,ot)s_{t}=(a_{t},u_{t},o_{t}), where ata_{t} is an action type, utu_{t} is a model-emitted payload, and oto_{t} is an optional runtime observation. We use a compact action vocabulary:

𝒜={READ,PLAN,CALL_CALC,OBSERVE,VERIFY,ANSWER}\mathcal{A}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\texttt{READ},\ \texttt{PLAN},\ \texttt{CALL\_CALC},\\ &\texttt{OBSERVE},\ \texttt{VERIFY},\ \texttt{ANSWER}\end{aligned}\right\}

The model generates reasoning actions and calculator-call payloads. Calculator observations are produced by a deterministic runtime rather than hallucinated by the model. The final prediction is extracted from the terminal answer action, y^=Ans⁡(τ)\hat{y}=\mathrm{Ans}(\tau).

3.2 Stage 1: TRACE

TRACE converts free-form rationales into executable action traces. The compiler 𝒞\mathcal{C} maps an example (x,r,y⋆)(x,r,y^{\star}) to a gold executable trajectory τ⋆=𝒞⁡(x,r,y⋆)\tau^{\star}=\mathcal{C}(x,r,y^{\star}). The compiler separates textual reasoning spans from arithmetic spans. Textual spans are mapped to actions such as READ, PLAN, and VERIFY. Arithmetic spans are normalized into calculator expressions and emitted as paired tool actions:

CALL_CALC​(et)→OBSERVE​(fcalc​(et)),\texttt{CALL\_CALC}(e_{t})\rightarrow\texttt{OBSERVE}(f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{t})),

where fcalcf_{\mathrm{calc}} is the calculator runtime. For GSM-8K, the compiler uses the dataset’s inline calculator annotations to identify arithmetic spans, executes each expression, and inserts the resulting observation into the trace. The trace is always terminated with a normalized gold answer. This metadata is not serialized into the model-visible prefix before ANSWER. Gold-answer metadata is neither visible when predicting intermediate actions, nor before the final answer token. It is removed during HiGRA rollout and evaluation and no verification step can directly copy the gold answer.

The student is then trained by supervised fine-tuning on compiled traces:

ℒTRACE​(θ)=−∑t∈ℳ⁡(τ⋆)logπθ(at⋆,ut⋆∣x,s<t⋆).\begin{gathered}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TRACE}}(\theta)=\\[-2.0pt] -\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}(\tau^{\star})}\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(a_{t}^{\star},u_{t}^{\star}\mid x,s_{<t}^{\star}\bigr).\end{gathered}

where ℳ⁡(τ⋆)\mathcal{M}(\tau^{\star}) denotes model-generated positions. Runtime observations are included in the context but are not treated as free-form tokens the model must hallucinate. This teaches the student to control the reasoning process while leaving exact arithmetic to the calculator runtime.

3.3 Stage 2: HiGRA

TRACE gives the student a structured executable interface, but supervised imitation alone can still produce missing tool calls, wrong calculator inputs, malformed traces, ignored observations, or premature answers. HiGRA addresses these failures by refining the TRACE policy using trajectory-level reinforcement learning. The goal is not only to increase final-answer accuracy, but also to improve the reliability of the executable reasoning process that leads to the answer.

A central design choice in HiGRA is its asymmetric distributed hierarchical reward structure i.e., a priority-weighted grouped reward with conditional tool scoring and gated trace alignment. Rather than treating all feedback signals as a flat collection of equally weighted micro-rewards, HiGRA separates trajectory quality into reward families with different responsibilities and priorities. Outcome correctness remains the dominant signal because the final answer must be correct. Tool grounding is the next most important signal because mathematical reasoning often fails when the model omits a needed calculator call, submits the wrong expression, or ignores the returned observation. Process discipline combines structural-format quality with separate signals for verification, brevity, final-answer presence, and premature termination. Trace alignment is used as the weakest signal: it regularizes the rollout toward the compiled TRACE structure without forcing exact imitation of the supervised trace.

This asymmetry is important because not every reward component should influence every trajectory in the same way. For example, alignment is useful only when the trajectory is already correct or sufficiently tool-grounded; otherwise, rewarding similarity to the compiled trace can reinforce superficial structure even when the computation is wrong. Similarly, tool-use feedback is conditioned on whether the compiled reference trace requires calculator use: required calls are rewarded, while unnecessary calls are discouraged. HiGRA therefore gates auxiliary rewards conditionally, so each reward family contributes only when it is relevant to the current trajectory. This makes HiGRA different from ordinary outcome-only reinforcement learning and from flat process-reward mixtures: it distributes credit across correctness, tool use, process quality, and trace compatibility, but applies these signals asymmetrically according to their reliability and importance.

For a sampled trajectory τ\tau, HiGRA computes a grouped reward:

RHiGRA​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}(\tau) =wout​Rout​(τ)+wtool​Rtool​(τ)\displaystyle=w_{\mathrm{out}}R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)+w_{\mathrm{tool}}R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau)
+wproc​Rproc​(τ)+walign​R~align​(τ)\displaystyle\quad+w_{\mathrm{proc}}R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau)+w_{\mathrm{align}}\widetilde{R}_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)
−Plen​(τ).\displaystyle\quad-P_{\mathrm{len}}(\tau). (1)

Here, RHiGRA​(τ)R_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}(\tau) denotes the total reward assigned to trajectory τ\tau. The outcome reward, Rout​(τ)R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau), measures final-answer correctness, and woutw_{\mathrm{out}} denotes its scalar weight. The tool-grounding reward, Rtool​(τ)R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau), is conditioned on whether the compiled reference trace requires calculator use and measures call presence, observation pairing, and consistency with deterministic execution; wtoolw_{\mathrm{tool}} is its corresponding weight. Malformed or non-executable calls are still counted as generated calls but receive no consistency credit. The process-discipline reward, Rproc​(τ)R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau), combines a fractional structural-format score with separate indicators for verification presence, brevity, final-answer presence, and premature termination, while wprocw_{\mathrm{proc}} controls its contribution. The gated alignment reward, R~align​(τ)\widetilde{R}_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau), softly regularizes the rollout toward the compiled TRACE structure and is weighted by walignw_{\mathrm{align}}; the tilde indicates that the underlying alignment reward is conditionally gated before being added to the total reward. Finally, Plen​(τ)P_{\mathrm{len}}(\tau) denotes the trajectory-length penalty, which discourages repetitive or overly long trajectories. Full operational definitions of the reward families, weights, gates, reported scores, and penalty are provided in Appendix A.

We optimize the TRACE-initialized policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Reinforcement Learning. For each prompt, we sample a group of trajectories, execute tool calls through the calculator runtime, score each trajectory with RHiGRAR_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}, and update the policy using group-relative advantages. This allows ARCHER to optimize non-differentiable trajectory properties such as answer extraction, calculator consistency, schema validity, and trace alignment without training a separate value model.

3.4 Inference

At inference time, ARCHER runs the model in the same executable loop used during training. The model emits one action at a time. Non-tool actions are appended directly to the transcript. When the model emits CALL_CALC, the calculator executes the expression and appends an OBSERVE action. The process stops when the model emits ANSWER or reaches a step budget. Thus, the model is evaluated as a calculator-grounded executable reasoning policy rather than as a free-form text generator.

Full implementation details, reward definitions, and the GRPO objective are provided in Appendix A.

3.5 Why ARCHER Uses Two Stages

TRACE and HiGRA play complementary roles. TRACE converts raw rationale supervision into an executable action language and gives the compact model an initial tool-using policy. HiGRA then improves that policy with rewards that evaluate complete executed trajectories. This separation is important because reward optimization from an unstructured policy is unstable, while supervised imitation alone can overfit to compiled traces and leave tool-use failures unresolved. ARCHER combines both: TRACE teaches the model how to produce executable reasoning traces, and HiGRA improves whether those traces solve the problem reliably.

4 Experimental Setup

Models and training.

We evaluate ARCHER on seven sub-10B backbones: Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B with thinking mode enabled (Yang et al., 2025), Gemma-4-E2B (Gemma Team, 2026), Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), Falcon-H1R-7B (Falcon LLM Team, 2026), DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (Guo et al., 2025), and MiMo-7B-RL (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025). The first five models form the main controlled comparison, while DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and MiMo-7B-RL test whether executable grounding complements reasoning-specialized initialization. On Falcon-H1R-7B, used for stage-wise analysis and ablations, we compare the released checkpoint, TRACE-only ARCHER w/o HiGRA, and full ARCHER. For the reasoning-specialized backbones, Vanilla, CoA, and ARCHER denote the released checkpoint, tool-augmented baseline, and complete TRACE-HiGRA pipeline, respectively. Training data, rewards, generation budgets, decoding, and evaluation are otherwise fixed; architecture-specific adaptations are described in Appendix G.

Training data and runtime.

TRACE compiles each example (x,r,y⋆)(x,r,y^{\star}) into a typed trajectory containing reasoning actions, calculator calls, deterministic observations, verification, and a terminal answer. For GSM-8K, using the official 7,473/1,319 train/test splits, inline calculator annotations identify arithmetic spans; expressions are normalized, executed, and inserted as OBSERVE actions. Runtime outputs condition subsequent generation but are not model-generated decisions. The same deterministic runtime executes CALL_CALC actions during HiGRA rollouts and evaluation. GSM-8K is used for all stage-wise comparisons, ablations, and trajectory diagnostics because its annotated solutions support evaluation of tool necessity, call construction, observation consistency, trace validity, and process structure; the remaining benchmarks measure answer-level transfer.

Benchmarks.

GSM-8K is the primary in-domain benchmark (Cobbe et al., 2021). We evaluate transfer to SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021), the mathematical subset of MMLU (MM) (Hendrycks et al., 2020), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and its representative MATH-500 subset Lightman et al. (2024). We further evaluate on the competition-level AIME-2024 and AIME-2025 sets (Balunović et al., 2025), and on multilingual PolyMATH (Wang et al., 2025).

Baselines and evaluation protocol.

For the five standard backbones, we compare ARCHER with CoT-FSP (Chain-of-Thought 3-shot Prompting without fine-tuning), CoT-FT (Chain-of-Thought Fine-Tuning), Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), and CoA Gao et al. (2024); for the reasoning-specialized backbones, we compare Vanilla, CoA, and ARCHER. All results are obtained from direct runs on identical benchmark instances with a shared normalization and scoring pipeline, while each method retains its native reasoning or tool-interaction format. The two comparison blocks are reported separately because their baselines and training histories differ. Each model produces one response or trajectory per example. ARCHER follows the executable loop in Section 3, terminating at ANSWER or the step limit; missing or invalid terminal answers are incorrect. Other methods use benchmark-specific answer extraction. Numeric, symbolic, and multiple-choice outputs are normalized before scoring.

Metrics.

Final-answer accuracy is the primary metric, with AIME results reported as single-run exact match over the complete sets. On GSM-8K, we additionally report Tool Score, tool precision and recall, observation consistency, Process Score, valid trace rate, trace edit distance, and reward-family diagnostics. Tool Score and Process Score are dataset-level macro-averages; valid trace rate measures conformity to the action schema, and observation consistency measures agreement with deterministic execution.

5 Results

We evaluate ARCHER along two dimensions: whether executable supervision improves reasoning correctness and trajectory validity on GSM-8K, and whether these gains transfer across model families and mathematical benchmarks.

ARCHER generalizes across model families.

In the five-backbone comparison in Table 1, ARCHER is strictly best in 39 of 40 backbone-benchmark combinations and tied for best on Falcon-H1R-7B for AIME-2024. Its mean score across the 40 cells is 73.36, compared with 67.85 for CoA, yielding an average improvement of 5.51 percentage points. Averaged across eight benchmarks, the gains over CoA are 6.02 points for Qwen3-1.7B, 5.50 for Gemma4-E2B, 5.29 for Qwen3.5-4B, 4.02 for Falcon-H1R-7B, and 6.71 for Qwen3-8B-thinking. The improvement therefore remains consistent across model families, sizes, and reasoning-oriented initializations.

Executable grounding complements reasoning-specialized models.

ARCHER also outperforms both Vanilla and CoA on every benchmark for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and MiMo-7B-RL. Relative to Vanilla, AIME-2024 accuracy increases from 63.33 to 80.00 for DeepSeek and from 70.00 to 83.33 for MiMo. PolyMATH improves from 28.91 to 37.04 and from 31.25 to 39.61, respectively, while gains on MATH-500 are smaller but remain positive. These results indicate that deterministic execution is not merely compensation for weak arithmetic ability. It provides additional reliability even when the backbone already exhibits strong reasoning behavior from reinforcement learning or distillation.

Improvements are largest on formal, multi-step benchmarks.

On the natural-language word-problem benchmarks GSM-8K and SVAMP, ARCHER averages 87.74 and 90.58 across the five standard backbones, improving over CoA by 4.03 and 4.39 points. Larger margins appear on benchmarks requiring longer symbolic derivations. ARCHER improves over CoA by 6.76 points on MATH and 8.95 points on MATH-500, with gains of 5.33 and 5.34 points on AIME-2024 and AIME-2025. This pattern suggests that action structure, runtime observations, and trajectory refinement support not only arithmetic execution but also strategy selection and consistency across extended solutions.

Language and knowledge remain distinct challenges.

ARCHER averages 58.29 on MM, improving over CoA by 4.30 points, but absolute performance remains below that on the arithmetic and competition benchmarks. This reflects the broader knowledge, interpretation, and multiple-choice reasoning required by MM. PolyMATH produces the lowest ARCHER average, 47.12, while still improving over CoA by 4.97 points. The result demonstrates multilingual transfer, but also shows that calculator grounding does not remove difficulties caused by language variation. More detailed language-wise analysis is needed to determine whether these gains are uniformly distributed.

Backbone specialization and training stages remain important.

Average ARCHER performance increases from 61.77 on Qwen3-1.7B to 70.26 on Gemma4-E2B, 72.78 on Qwen3.5-4B, 80.68 on Falcon-H1R-7B, and 81.32 on Qwen3-8B-thinking. However, benchmark-level rankings do not follow parameter count alone. Qwen3-8B-thinking performs best on GSM-8K, SVAMP, MATH, and MATH-500, whereas Falcon-H1R-7B is strongest on MM, AIME-2024, and PolyMATH, with both models tied on AIME-2025. Figure 2 further shows that TRACE provides rapid early improvement, while HiGRA continues improving after the supervised model begins to plateau. Together, these results support the two-stage design: TRACE establishes structured executable reasoning, and HiGRA converts that structure into stronger accuracy, grounding, and trajectory validity.

6 Ablation Study

All ablations use Falcon-H1R-7B on GSM-8K, whose annotated arithmetic solutions enable detailed evaluation of tool use and executable trajectory quality. We isolate the effects of TRACE, HiGRA, alternative reward formulations, and individual reward components in Table 3. Additional executable-trajectory diagnostics are provided in Appendix B.

TRACE establishes executable behavior, while HiGRA drives accuracy.

Table 2 separates the contributions of the two stages. TRACE increases accuracy from 77.40 to 79.06 while producing larger improvements in trajectory quality: valid trace rate rises from 41.2 to 68.7, Tool Score from 0.00 to 0.46, and Process Score from 0.52 to 0.67; tool recall and observation consistency reach 0.58 and 0.84. Full ARCHER increases accuracy to 85.96, raises valid trace rate to 82.4, and improves observation consistency to 0.93. Thus, TRACE establishes the executable interface, while HiGRA improves its correct and consistent use.

Training target and reward design.

Table 3 shows that CoT-SFT provides only a small accuracy gain over the base model, from 77.40 to 78.12, with little improvement in tool or process scores. ARCHER w/o HiGRA reaches 79.06 and produces substantially stronger executable behavior, showing that the benefit of Stage 1 comes from replacing free-form rationale imitation with executable action supervision. Reward-guided refinement further improves performance: outcome-only GRPO reaches 82.35 and flat micro-reward GRPO reaches 83.10, whereas full ARCHER achieves 85.96. This supports HiGRA’s grouped rewards and conditional gating over outcome-only or flat reward formulations.

Component contributions and gating.

Removing the tool reward causes the largest component-level accuracy drop, from 85.96 to 81.74, confirming that explicit tool grounding is central to ARCHER’s gains. Removing the process reward lowers accuracy to 82.18 and Process Score from 0.79 to 0.61, while removing alignment has the smallest effect, reducing accuracy to 84.12 and supporting its role as a weak stabilizer. Removing gating lowers accuracy to 82.95 and reduces both tool and process scores, indicating that auxiliary reward families should contribute only when relevant; otherwise, they can introduce noisy or conflicting optimization pressure.

7 Conclusion and Future Work

We presented ARCHER, a two-stage framework combining executable trace supervision with reward-guided refinement. Stage 1 compiles free-form rationales into typed action traces containing calculator calls, runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers, while Stage 2 refines this policy with grouped and conditionally gated rewards over correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. On Falcon-H1R-7B, ARCHER improves GSM-8K accuracy from 77.40 to 85.96 while also improving tool recall, observation consistency, valid trace rate, and process quality. Across five standard backbones, ARCHER is best or tied-best in all 40 model-benchmark comparisons and improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 points on average. It also improves both DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and MiMo-7B-RL across all eight benchmarks, showing that deterministic calculator execution remains complementary to reasoning capabilities induced through reinforcement learning or distillation.

Future work can extend ARCHER in three directions. First, the action space can be expanded beyond calculator calls to include symbolic solvers, unit converters, code execution, retrieval, and proof checking, enabling richer forms of executable reasoning. Second, TRACE can be generalized from rule-based arithmetic trace compilation to broader trace construction pipelines that handle more diverse rationale formats and reasoning domains. Third, HiGRA can be further improved through automatic reward calibration, adaptive gating, and model-specific reward weighting. These extensions would test whether the same principle behind ARCHER, aligning reasoning supervision with executable intermediate computation, can improve SLMs across a wider range of tasks.

Limitations

ARCHER is evaluated primarily in mathematical reasoning settings where intermediate computations can be executed and final answers can be checked reliably. This makes the setting well suited for studying calculator-grounded reasoning, but it also means that the current results should be interpreted most directly for tasks with verifiable numerical or symbolic structure. The current implementation uses a deterministic TRACE compiler and manually designed HiGRA reward families, so broader domains may require richer action schemas, additional tools, and task-specific reward calibration. We view these as natural extensions of the framework rather than fundamental restrictions, since ARCHER is designed around the general idea of training compact models to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories.

Disclosure of AI Assistant Use

The authors used LLM-based writing assistants to revise and improve portions of the manuscript prose based on text originally written by the authors. The authors retained full responsibility for the scientific content of the paper, including the research ideas, technical approach, experiments, results, and conclusions. All AI-assisted revisions were carefully inspected by the authors for accuracy, and the manuscript was manually checked to ensure that no hallucinated, fabricated, or unsupported content was introduced. GPT-Codex and Claude Code Coding Agents were used to assist with implementation and debugging for some parts of the experimental codebase.

Ethical Considerations

ARCHER is a research framework for mathematical reasoning and is not intended for safety-critical decision making. Although executable traces improve inspectability, they may still contain incorrect decompositions, calculator inputs, or uses of correct observations. Apparent trace structure should therefore not be treated as a guarantee of correctness, and outputs should be independently verified in high-stakes settings. Training and evaluating multiple language models also incurs computational and environmental costs, although all experiments in this study were conducted locally on a single Apple M5 Pro system without external compute clusters. The study uses existing mathematical reasoning benchmarks and does not collect personal data.
