Appendix A Full ARCHER Methodology

This appendix gives the full technical description of ARCHER: Action-trace Reinforcement for Calculator-grounded Hierarchical Executable Reasoning. ARCHER consists of two stages. TRACE constructs executable supervision from legacy rationales and trains the initial policy. HiGRA refines the TRACE policy with grouped and gated trajectory rewards.

A.1 Problem Setting

Each training example is represented as (x,r,y⋆)(x,r,y^{\star}), where xx is the input problem, rr is a free-form rationale or chain-of-thought solution, and y⋆y^{\star} is the gold final answer. The goal is to train a compact student policy πθ\pi_{\theta} that generates a structured trajectory τ\tau and final answer y^\hat{y}:

πθ:x↦(τ,y^).\pi_{\theta}:x\mapsto(\tau,\hat{y}).

Unlike ordinary rationale distillation, ARCHER does not train the student to imitate raw explanatory text. Instead, it trains the student to operate in an executable action language with explicit calculator calls and deterministic runtime observations.

A.2 Executable Action Language

A trajectory is a sequence of structured states:

τ=(s1,s2,…,sT),st=(at,ut,ot).\tau=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{T}),\qquad s_{t}=(a_{t},u_{t},o_{t}).

Here, ata_{t} is an action type, utu_{t} is the model-emitted payload, and oto_{t} is the observation returned by the runtime when the action invokes a tool. ARCHER uses the action vocabulary

𝒜={READ,PLAN,CALL_CALC,OBSERVE,VERIFY,ANSWER}\mathcal{A}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\texttt{READ},\ \texttt{PLAN},\ \texttt{CALL\_CALC},\\ &\texttt{OBSERVE},\ \texttt{VERIFY},\ \texttt{ANSWER}\end{aligned}\right\}

The final prediction is extracted from the terminal answer action:

y^=Ans⁡(τ).\hat{y}=\mathrm{Ans}(\tau).

A.3 Stage 1: TRACE

TRACE is the supervised compilation stage of ARCHER. It converts a free-form rationale into a calculator-grounded executable trace:

τ⋆=𝒞⁡(x,r,y⋆),\tau^{\star}=\mathcal{C}(x,r,y^{\star}),

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the TRACE compiler.

A.3.1 Trace Compilation

The compiler segments the rationale into textual reasoning spans and arithmetic spans. Textual spans are mapped to reasoning actions such as READ, PLAN, and VERIFY. Arithmetic spans are normalized into executable calculator expressions. For each extracted expression ete_{t}, TRACE emits:

st⋆\displaystyle s_{t}^{\star} =(CALL_CALC,et,∅),\displaystyle=(\texttt{CALL\_CALC},e_{t},\varnothing),
st+1⋆\displaystyle s_{t+1}^{\star} =(OBSERVE,∅,fcalc​(et)).\displaystyle=(\texttt{OBSERVE},\varnothing,f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{t})).

Here, fcalcf_{\mathrm{calc}} is the deterministic calculator runtime. For example, a rationale fragment containing the operation 48/6=848/6=8 is converted into:

CALL_CALC​(48/6)→OBSERVE​(8).\texttt{CALL\_CALC}(48/6)\rightarrow\texttt{OBSERVE}(8).

For GSM-8K, the compiler uses the dataset’s inline calculator format, << expr = result >>, to identify arithmetic spans. Each expression is normalized, executed, and paired with the resulting observation. Text outside calculator annotations is retained as reasoning content and mapped into structured actions.

A.3.2 Compiler Policy

The TRACE compiler is deterministic and rule-based. It does not use an external LLM to rewrite or repair rationales. The compiler follows a retain-and-annotate policy:

  • •

    Examples with valid calculator spans are converted into executable traces.

  • •

    Examples without calculator spans are still converted into structured traces when possible.

  • •

    Arithmetic mismatches are repaired at the observation level when exact execution succeeds.

  • •

    Unsupported calculator spans are retained with compiler metadata.

  • •

    Each trace is terminated with the normalized gold answer.

This policy avoids discarding useful training examples while preserving metadata for later filtering and analysis.

A.3.3 Calculator Runtime

The calculator runtime separates numerical execution from reasoning control. If the model emits a calculator call with payload ete_{t}, the runtime returns:

ot=fcalc​(et).o_{t}=f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{t}).

The observation is inserted into the transcript and becomes part of the context for subsequent model actions. The model therefore learns what to compute and how to use the result, while the runtime performs exact arithmetic.

A.3.4 Student Policy

The student policy generates action types and payloads autoregressively:

πθ(at,ut∣x,s<t).\pi_{\theta}(a_{t},u_{t}\mid x,s_{<t}).

The trajectory distribution is:

πθ(τ∣x)=∏t∈ℳ⁡(τ)πθ(at,ut∣x,s<t),\pi_{\theta}(\tau\mid x)=\prod_{t\in\mathcal{M}(\tau)}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t},u_{t}\mid x,s_{<t}),

where ℳ⁡(τ)\mathcal{M}(\tau) is the set of model-generated positions. Runtime observations are not sampled from the language model and are not treated as model decisions.

A.3.5 TRACE Supervised Fine-tuning

Given a compiled gold trace τ⋆=(s1⋆,…,sT⋆⋆)\tau^{\star}=(s_{1}^{\star},\dots,s_{T^{\star}}^{\star}), TRACE trains the student with:

ℒTRACE​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TRACE}}(\theta) =−∑t∈ℳ⁡(τ⋆)\displaystyle=-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}(\tau^{\star})}
logπθ(at⋆,ut⋆∣x,s<t⋆).\displaystyle\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}^{\star},u_{t}^{\star}\mid x,s_{<t}^{\star}).

Runtime observations are included in the teacher-forced context, but the loss is applied only to model-generated positions. This preserves the distinction between decisions made by the policy and observations produced by external execution.

A.3.6 TRACE Inference Loop

At inference time, the TRACE-trained policy runs iteratively. At step tt, the model emits an action and payload:

(at,ut)∼πθ(⋅∣x,s<t).(a_{t},u_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,s_{<t}).

The runtime observation is:

ot={fcalc​(ut),if ​at=CALL_CALC,∅,otherwise.o_{t}=\begin{cases}f_{\mathrm{calc}}(u_{t}),&\text{if }a_{t}=\texttt{CALL\_CALC},\\ \varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The resulting state is appended to the trajectory. The process continues until the model emits ANSWER or reaches the maximum step budget.

A.4 Stage 2: HiGRA

HiGRA is the reward-guided refinement stage of ARCHER. It starts from the TRACE policy and improves it using trajectory-level rewards. The purpose of HiGRA is to correct failures that supervised trace imitation alone may not remove, including missing calculator calls, wrong expressions, ignored observations, malformed traces, and premature answers.

A.4.1 Reward Families

HiGRA groups fine-grained feedback into four macro-reward families:

Rout,Rtool,Rproc,Ralign.R_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{tool}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{proc}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{align}}.

The outcome reward measures final-answer correctness. The tool reward measures calculator use and execution faithfulness. The process reward measures trajectory validity and discipline. The alignment reward softly encourages compatibility with the compiled TRACE supervision.

A.4.2 Outcome Reward

The outcome reward is:

Rout(τ)=𝟏[y^=y⋆].R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)=\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}=y^{\star}].

This is the primary task reward and anchors optimization to answer correctness.

A.4.3 Tool-grounding Reward and Tool Score

Let c⋆c^{\star} be the number of calculator calls in the compiled reference trace τ⋆\tau^{\star}, and let mm be the number of CALL_CALC actions emitted by the model in trajectory τ\tau. Define

uneed=𝟏[c⋆>0],uused=𝟏[m>0].u_{\mathrm{need}}=\mathbf{1}[c^{\star}>0],\qquad u_{\mathrm{used}}=\mathbf{1}[m>0].

For the emitted calls, let eie_{i} be the payload of call ii and let oio_{i} be its parser-paired observation, when present. Define

uobs\displaystyle u_{\mathrm{obs}} =1max⁡(m,1)∑i=1m\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\max(m,1)}\sum_{i=1}^{m}
𝟏​[call ​i​ has a paired observation].\displaystyle\mathbf{1}[\text{call }i\text{ has a paired observation}].

and

ucons=1max⁡(m,1)∑i=1m𝟏[oi=fcalc(ei)].u_{\mathrm{cons}}=\frac{1}{\max(m,1)}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}[o_{i}=f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{i})].

The per-trajectory tool reward is

Rtool​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau) =0.2​uused+0.2​uobs\displaystyle=0.2u_{\mathrm{used}}+0.2u_{\mathrm{obs}} (A.1)
+0.6​ucons,\displaystyle+0.6u_{\mathrm{cons}}, uneed=1,\displaystyle u_{\mathrm{need}}=1,
Rtool​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau) =1−0.2​uused,\displaystyle=1-0.2u_{\mathrm{used}}, uneed=0.\displaystyle u_{\mathrm{need}}=0.

Thus, when the compiled reference trace requires calculator use, the reward assigns credit for emitting at least one calculator call, pairing emitted calls with observations, and maintaining consistency with deterministic calculator execution. When the reference trace does not require calculator use, a trajectory receives full tool credit for avoiding the calculator and a penalty of 0.20.2 for emitting one or more unnecessary calls.

Every emitted CALL_CALC action contributes to mm, including malformed, empty, and non-executable calls. Such calls receive no consistency credit. A parser-paired runtime-error observation can receive observation-presence credit, but it receives no consistency credit. The consistency indicator is defined to be zero whenever the submitted expression cannot be parsed or executed.

For an evaluation set DD, the reported Tool Score is the macro-average

ToolScore⁡(D)=1|D|​∑τ∈DRtool​(τ).\mathrm{ToolScore}(D)=\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{\tau\in D}R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau). (A.2)

A.4.4 Process-discipline Reward and Process Score

Process discipline separates structural-format quality from verification presence, trajectory length, final-answer presence, and premature termination. Let 𝒦⁡(τ)\mathcal{K}(\tau) denote the set of structural checks applicable to trajectory τ\tau, let K⁡(τ)=|𝒦⁡(τ)|K(\tau)=|\mathcal{K}(\tau)|, and let

qk​(τ)∈{0,1}q_{k}(\tau)\in\{0,1\}

indicate whether applicable structural check kk passes. The structural-format score is

pfmt​(τ)=1K⁡(τ)​∑k∈𝒦⁡(τ)qk​(τ).p_{\mathrm{fmt}}(\tau)=\frac{1}{K(\tau)}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(\tau)}q_{k}(\tau). (A.3)

The structural checks cover:

  • •

    recognized and parseable action tags;

  • •

    valid payloads for the corresponding action types;

  • •

    nonempty and parseable CALL_CALC expressions;

  • •

    exactly one paired OBSERVE action for each calculator call;

  • •

    no orphan or duplicated observations;

  • •

    at most one ANSWER action;

  • •

    a terminal ANSWER action when an answer is present;

  • •

    no unknown action tags; and

  • •

    no unparsed residual text.

The implementation applies at least one structural check to every trajectory, so K⁡(τ)≥1K(\tau)\geq 1. The format score measures structural format only. Verification presence, answer presence, length, and premature termination are represented separately:

pverify​(τ)\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{verify}}(\tau) =𝟏[VERIFY∈τ],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\texttt{VERIFY}\in\tau],
pshort​(τ)\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{short}}(\tau) =𝟏[T≤Tmax],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[T\leq T_{\max}],
pfinal​(τ)\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{final}}(\tau) =𝟏[ANSWER∈τ],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\texttt{ANSWER}\in\tau],
pprem​(τ)\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{prem}}(\tau) =𝟏​[premature final answer].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\text{premature final answer}].

The per-trajectory process reward is

qproc​(τ)\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau) =0.4​pfmt​(τ)+0.2​pverify​(τ)\displaystyle=0.4p_{\mathrm{fmt}}(\tau)+0.2p_{\mathrm{verify}}(\tau) (A.4)
+0.2​pshort​(τ)+0.2​pfinal​(τ)\displaystyle+0.2p_{\mathrm{short}}(\tau)+0.2p_{\mathrm{final}}(\tau)
−0.5​pprem​(τ),\displaystyle-0.5p_{\mathrm{prem}}(\tau),
Rproc​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau) =clip[0,1]⁡(qproc​(τ)).\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\left(q_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau)\right).

where

clip[0,1]⁡(z)=min⁡(1,max⁡(0,z)).\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}(z)=\min(1,\max(0,z)).

The binary shortness component is part of the process-discipline reward. The separate soft length penalty PlenP_{\mathrm{len}} in the total HiGRA reward measures how far an overlong trajectory exceeds the preferred trajectory budget.

For an evaluation set DD, the reported Process Score is the macro-average

ProcessScore⁡(D)=1|D|​∑τ∈DRproc​(τ).\mathrm{ProcessScore}(D)=\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{\tau\in D}R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau). (A.5)

A.4.5 Trace-alignment Reward

Trace alignment softly regularizes the rollout toward the compiled executable trace without requiring exact imitation. Let 𝒮⁡(τ)\mathcal{S}(\tau) and 𝒮⋆\mathcal{S}^{\star} denote the generated and gold action schemas, and let 𝒪⁡(τ)\mathcal{O}(\tau) and 𝒪⋆\mathcal{O}^{\star} denote the generated and gold operation sequences. Define:

aschema=|𝒮⁡(τ)∩𝒮⋆||𝒮⋆|+ε,a_{\mathrm{schema}}=\frac{|\mathcal{S}(\tau)\cap\mathcal{S}^{\star}|}{|\mathcal{S}^{\star}|+\varepsilon},
aop=|𝒪⁡(τ)∩𝒪⋆||𝒪⋆|+ε,a_{\mathrm{op}}=\frac{|\mathcal{O}(\tau)\cap\mathcal{O}^{\star}|}{|\mathcal{O}^{\star}|+\varepsilon},

and

averify\displaystyle a_{\mathrm{verify}} =𝟏​[gold trace expects verification]\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\text{gold trace expects verification}]
⋅𝟏[VERIFY∈τ].\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\cdot\mathbf{1}[\texttt{VERIFY}\in\tau].

The alignment reward is:

Ralign​(τ)=δ1​aschema+δ2​aop+δ3​averify.R_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)=\delta_{1}a_{\mathrm{schema}}+\delta_{2}a_{\mathrm{op}}+\delta_{3}a_{\mathrm{verify}}.

This term is intentionally weaker than outcome, tool, and process rewards.

A.4.6 Hierarchical Gating

HiGRA gates auxiliary rewards so that irrelevant reward dimensions do not contribute uniformly to every trajectory. Tool grounding is naturally gated by tool necessity through uneedu_{\mathrm{need}}. Alignment is also gated:

R~align​(τ)=galign​(τ)​Ralign​(τ),\widetilde{R}_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)=g_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)R_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau),

where

galign(τ)=𝟏[Rout(τ)=1∨Rtool(τ)>η].g_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)=\mathbf{1}[R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)=1\vee R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau)>\eta].

Thus, alignment is emphasized only when the trajectory is already correct or shows sufficient tool-grounded structure.

A.4.7 Length and Loop Penalty

To discourage repetitive or overly long trajectories, HiGRA uses a soft length penalty:

Plen​(τ)=λlen​max⁡(0,T−TmaxTmax).P_{\mathrm{len}}(\tau)=\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}\max\left(0,\frac{T-T_{\max}}{T_{\max}}\right).

This is smoother than a hard failure condition and is better suited to compact policies.

A.4.8 Final HiGRA Reward

The final HiGRA reward is:

RHiGRA​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}(\tau) =wout​Rout​(τ)\displaystyle=w_{\mathrm{out}}R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)
+wtool​Rtool​(τ)\displaystyle+w_{\mathrm{tool}}R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau)
+wproc​Rproc​(τ)\displaystyle+w_{\mathrm{proc}}R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau)
+walign​R~align​(τ)\displaystyle+w_{\mathrm{align}}\widetilde{R}_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)
−Plen​(τ).\displaystyle-P_{\mathrm{len}}(\tau).

The weights follow the priority ordering:

wout>wtool>wproc>walign.w_{\mathrm{out}}>w_{\mathrm{tool}}>w_{\mathrm{proc}}>w_{\mathrm{align}}.

In our experiments, we use:

wout\displaystyle w_{\mathrm{out}} =2.0,\displaystyle=2.0, wtool\displaystyle\qquad w_{\mathrm{tool}} =1.0,\displaystyle=1.0,
wproc\displaystyle w_{\mathrm{proc}} =0.5,\displaystyle=0.5, walign\displaystyle\qquad w_{\mathrm{align}} =0.25.\displaystyle=0.25.

A.5 Policy Optimization with GRPO

HiGRA starts from the TRACE-supervised policy πθSFT\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{SFT}}. Given an input xx, the current policy samples a group of GG trajectories:

{τ(1),…,τ(G)}∼πϕold(⋅∣x).\{\tau^{(1)},\dots,\tau^{(G)}\}\sim\pi_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x).

Each trajectory is executed through the calculator runtime and scored:

ri=RHiGRA​(τ(i)).r_{i}=R_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}(\tau^{(i)}).

The group mean and standard deviation are:

r¯\displaystyle\bar{r} =1G​∑i=1Gri,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}r_{i},
σr\displaystyle\sigma_{r} =1G​∑i=1G(ri−r¯)2+ϵ.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}(r_{i}-\bar{r})^{2}+\epsilon}.

The group-relative advantage is:

Ai=ri−r¯σr.A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\bar{r}}{\sigma_{r}}.

For token zi,tz_{i,t} in trajectory τ(i)\tau^{(i)}, define the importance ratio:

ρi,t=πϕ​(zi,t∣x,zi,<t)πϕold​(zi,t∣x,zi,<t).\rho_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\phi}(z_{i,t}\mid x,z_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}(z_{i,t}\mid x,z_{i,<t})}.

The clipped ratio is:

ρ¯i,t=clip⁡(ρi,t,1−ε,1+ε).\bar{\rho}_{i,t}=\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon).

The GRPO loss is:

ℒGRPO​(ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\phi) =−𝔼x[1G∑i=1G1|τ(i)|∑t=1|τ(i)|\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{x}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau^{(i)}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|\tau^{(i)}|}
min(ρi,tAi,ρ¯i,tAi)].\displaystyle\min\left(\rho_{i,t}A_{i},\bar{\rho}_{i,t}A_{i}\right)\Bigg].

This objective increases the likelihood of trajectories whose HiGRA reward is higher than the group average while clipping overly large policy updates.

Appendix B Additional ARCHER Diagnostic Results

This appendix reports additional diagnostics for ARCHER that support the main results but are not required in the main body. The goal is to separate answer-level gains from improvements in executable reasoning behavior, including trace validity, calculator use, observation consistency, first-error position, and reward-family behavior. In these diagnostic tables, w/o HiGRA denotes the Stage 1-only ARCHER variant.

Structural and tool-use metrics.

Table B.1 reports whether the model produces executable traces and uses calculator calls faithfully. Accuracy measures final-answer correctness. NEDact and NEDop are normalized edit distances to the compiled gold action and operation sequences, so lower values indicate closer alignment with the target executable trace. Valid Trace is the percentage of outputs that follow the expected action format. Tool precision measures whether emitted tool calls are appropriate, tool recall measures whether needed calls are made, and observation consistency measures agreement between recorded observations and deterministic calculator outputs.

The main inference is that TRACE changes the form of the model’s reasoning: valid traces increase from 41.2 to 68.7, and tool recall rises from 0.00 to 0.58. HiGRA then improves reliability within that format, raising valid trace rate to 82.4, tool recall to 0.79, and observation consistency to 0.93. Thus, the final accuracy gain is accompanied by cleaner execution behavior.

First-error position.

Table B.2 shows where trajectories first become incorrect. No Error is the percentage of examples without a detected reasoning failure. Early Error refers to failures during problem understanding or planning. Tool-Step Error refers to failures in calculator-call construction or observation handling. Post-Tool Error refers to failures after a correct tool observation has already been produced. Mean First-Error Pos. is normalized from 0 to 1, where larger values mean the first error occurs later in the trajectory.

The key pattern is that TRACE reduces early failures and moves the first error later, but it also exposes more tool-step errors because the model now attempts explicit calculator use. HiGRA reduces both early errors and tool-step errors, and the mean first-error position increases from 0.38 to 0.64. This indicates that ARCHER improves not only final correctness but also the durability of the reasoning process.

Reward-family correlation.

Table B.3 measures how strongly each reward family is associated with final-answer correctness. Correlation measures linear association with correctness, while AUC measures how well a reward score separates correct from incorrect trajectories. RoutR_{\mathrm{out}} has perfect association because it directly encodes answer correctness. The auxiliary rewards are not expected to be perfect predictors, but they should still correlate with better trajectories.

The auxiliary rewards follow the intended ordering. Tool grounding is the strongest auxiliary signal, process discipline is moderately predictive, and trace alignment is weaker but still useful as a stabilizer. The combined HiGRA reward has higher correlation and AUC than any individual auxiliary reward, supporting the grouped reward design.

Objective comparison.

Table B.4 compares different training objectives. Acc. is final-answer accuracy, Tool is the aggregate tool-use score, Proc. is the process-discipline score, Valid is valid trace rate, and Obs. is observation consistency.

The numbers show that ordinary CoT-SFT provides only a small gain over the base model and does not meaningfully improve tool behavior. TRACE-SFT improves trace validity and observation consistency, confirming that the executable supervision format matters. Outcome-only GRPO improves accuracy, but full HiGRA performs best across all metrics because it rewards correctness together with tool grounding and process discipline.

TRACE compiler outcomes.

Table B.5 summarizes compiler outcomes on the GSM-8K training split. The ok category indicates examples with successfully compiled executable traces. calc_only indicates examples where the compiler primarily recovered calculator structure. no_calc_blocks indicates examples without explicit GSM-8K calculator annotations. unsupported_exec indicates examples with calculator spans that could not be executed by the current runtime.

The compiler statistics show that TRACE covers most of the training split: 95.01 percent of prepared examples compile successfully. The remaining cases are small but useful to report because they clarify that the compiler follows a retain-and-annotate policy rather than silently dropping difficult examples.

Appendix C TRACE Compiler in ARCHER: Operational Details

This appendix details the TRACE compiler used in Stage 1 of ARCHER. The high-level description of TRACE as a “trace compiler” is intentionally simple, but the actual compilation pipeline is fully deterministic and rule-based in the current implementation. It takes a prepared GSM-8K row and converts it into a structured TraceExample containing:

(\displaystyle\big( id,split,x,rraw,y⋆,\displaystyle\texttt{id},\ \texttt{split},\ x,\ r_{\mathrm{raw}},\ y^{\star},
OPEN𝒮⋆,τ⋆,compiler_status,metadata).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{\star},\ \tau^{\star},\ \texttt{compiler\_status},\ \texttt{metadata}\big).

where:

  • •

    xx is the question,

  • •

    rrawr_{\mathrm{raw}} is the original answer string from GSM-8K,

  • •

    y⋆y^{\star} is the parsed gold final answer,

  • •

    𝒮⋆\mathcal{S}^{\star} is the set of inferred schema tags,

  • •

    τ⋆\tau^{\star} is the compiled action trace.

C.1 Compiler Type: Rule-Based Rather than Model-Assisted

The current compiler is rule-based, not model-assisted. It does not invoke an external LLM to repair or reinterpret rationales. Instead, it uses deterministic parsing rules, regular expressions, whitespace normalization, numeric canonicalization, and exact calculator execution. This design choice is deliberate: the project aims to reduce dependence on large teachers and to produce executable supervision from existing dataset rationales alone.

Formally, the compiler is a deterministic mapping

𝒞:(x,rraw,y⋆)↦τ⋆,\mathcal{C}:(x,r_{\mathrm{raw}},y^{\star})\mapsto\tau^{\star},

implemented through symbolic preprocessing and exact execution rather than learned sequence transduction.

C.2 Detection of Arithmetic Spans

Arithmetic spans are detected through the GSM-8K convention of inline calculator blocks:

<< expr = result >>.\texttt{<< expr = result >>}.

The parser uses a regular expression of the form

<< expr = result >>

to locate each arithmetic block inside the rationale. If a match is found, the compiler extracts:

  • •

    the raw arithmetic expression expr,

  • •

    the rationale-provided numeric result result,

  • •

    the span boundaries in the original rationale.

Let the rationale be rr. The parser decomposes it into an ordered sequence of pieces:

Split⁡(r)=(p1,p2,…,pM),\mathrm{Split}(r)=(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{M}),

where each pjp_{j} is either:

  • •

    a text segment, or

  • •

    a calc segment corresponding to one matched arithmetic block.

Text segments become reason actions, while calculator segments become paired

tool_call→tool_observation\texttt{tool\_call}\rightarrow\texttt{tool\_observation}

actions.

Limitation of the current detector.

Only arithmetic explicitly marked in the GSM-8K-style inline format is guaranteed to be externalized. Arithmetic implied only in prose but not wrapped in `<<⋅>>``<<\cdot>>` is not converted into executable tool calls in the current compiler. Such spans remain plain reasoning text. As a result, some examples may receive the status no_calc_blocks even if arithmetic is conceptually present.

C.3 Expression and Number Normalization

Before execution, the compiler normalizes both extracted expressions and numeric results.

Whitespace normalization.

All extracted arithmetic expressions are compacted by collapsing repeated whitespace:

e=CompactWS⁡(eraw).e=\mathrm{CompactWS}(e_{\mathrm{raw}}).

This ensures that syntactic variants such as

48 / 6,48/6,48 / 6\texttt{48 / 6},\qquad\texttt{48/6},\qquad\texttt{48 / 6}

map to a stable expression form.

Numeric normalization.

Rationale-provided results and final answers are canonicalized using decimal parsing. Let vv denote a numeric string. The normalization function

NormNum⁡(v)\mathrm{NormNum}(v)

performs the following:

  1. 1.

    remove commas,

  2. 2.

    strip trailing decimal points,

  3. 3.

    parse the value using decimal arithmetic,

  4. 4.

    if the value is integral, render it as an integer string,

  5. 5.

    otherwise remove redundant trailing zeros.

For example:

"1,200.0"\displaystyle\texttt{"1,200.0"} ↦"1200",\displaystyle\mapsto\texttt{"1200"},
"8.500"\displaystyle\texttt{"8.500"} ↦"8.5".\displaystyle\mapsto\texttt{"8.5"}.

This same normalization is used for final answer parsing and for rationale-provided arithmetic results, which ensures consistent comparison across compiled traces, tool observations, and evaluation outputs.

C.4 Handling of Unsupported or Ambiguous Rationale Spans

The current compiler is conservative. It does not attempt to infer hidden arithmetic from ambiguous prose, nor does it rewrite unsupported spans into executable expressions using a learned model.

Instead, unsupported or ambiguous spans are handled as follows:

  1. 1.

    if a rationale segment is plain text, it is retained as a reason action,

  2. 2.

    if an arithmetic block is present but the expression cannot be executed exactly by the calculator, the compiler still emits a tool_call with the extracted payload and stores the rationale-provided result in the observation,

  3. 3.

    the observation metadata is marked with a status of the form

    calc_error:ExceptionType.\texttt{calc\_error:ExceptionType}.

Thus, the compiler never drops the surrounding example solely because one arithmetic block is unsupported. Instead, it degrades gracefully by preserving the action structure and annotating the observation status.

C.5 Repair of Rationale Arithmetic

TRACE explicitly checks whether the rationale-provided result agrees with exact execution. Let ete_{t} be an extracted expression and let

rtexpr_{t}^{\mathrm{exp}}

be the result written in the rationale. The compiler computes

rtact=fcalc​(et).r_{t}^{\mathrm{act}}=f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{t}).

If execution succeeds and the repair_equation_result option is enabled, then:

rtfinal={rtact,if ​rtact≠rtexp,rtexp,otherwise.r_{t}^{\mathrm{final}}=\begin{cases}r_{t}^{\mathrm{act}},&\text{if }r_{t}^{\mathrm{act}}\neq r_{t}^{\mathrm{exp}},\\ r_{t}^{\mathrm{exp}},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

When a mismatch occurs, the observation metadata is marked as

status="repaired".\texttt{status}=\texttt{"repaired"}.

This means that the compiler can correct arithmetic slips inside the legacy rationale while preserving the overall reasoning skeleton. In other words, TRACE does not merely copy rationale text. It checks arithmetic spans against an exact executor and repairs them when possible.

C.6 Compiler Status and Compilation Outcomes

Every prepared row is compiled into a serialized trace example. The current implementation therefore treats compilation as a total transformation rather than a binary success-or-failure filter. Instead of dropping rows, it assigns a categorical compiler status:

  • •

    ok: at least one executable calculator block and at least one reasoning-text span are extracted;

  • •

    calc_only: executable calculator blocks are extracted, but no reasoning-text span remains;

  • •

    no_calc_blocks: no inline calculator block is detected;

  • •

    unsupported_exec: at least one calculator block is detected but cannot be executed by the current runtime.

Hence, all prepared examples produce an output trace, but the compiler_status records the degree to which the rationale could be externalized into tool-using form.

All prepared examples produce a serialized trace, and compiler outcomes are summarized using status-specific counts rather than a binary compilation-success indicator. all examples are retained in the compiled artifact for auditing, but only ok and calc_only are retained for training. No additional filtering is applied beyond this policy.

C.7 Dropped, Repaired, or Retained Examples

The current compiler follows a retain-and-annotate policy:

  • •

    examples are retained even if no calculator block is found,

  • •

    arithmetic mismatches are repaired when exact execution succeeds and repair is enabled,

  • •

    unsupported execution spans are retained with error metadata rather than removed.

Therefore:

  • •

    failed compilations are not dropped by default,

  • •

    ambiguous spans are not rewritten by a learned repair model,

  • •

    arithmetic mismatches are repaired only at the observation level, not by re-authoring the entire trace.

C.8 Gold Final Answer Handling

The final answer in the compiled trace is forced to match the gold answer parsed from the GSM-8K annotation. Let the raw GSM-8K answer string be rrawr_{\mathrm{raw}}. The gold answer is extracted from the standard marker

#### ​y⋆,\texttt{\#\#\#\# }y^{\star},

and then normalized numerically:

y⋆=ParseFinal⁡(rraw).y^{\star}=\mathrm{ParseFinal}(r_{\mathrm{raw}}).

The compiler strips this terminal answer marker from the rationale text before creating intermediate actions, but the final compiled trace always ends with

final_answer=y⋆.\texttt{final\_answer}=y^{\star}.

In addition, when the verify step is included, the compiler inserts the gold answer into verification metadata:

metadata​[gold_final_answer]=y⋆.\texttt{metadata}[\texttt{gold\_final\_answer}]=y^{\star}.

Thus, the compiled supervision does not ask the student to recover the terminal answer purely from the legacy rationale string. Instead, it presents the student with a cleaned executable trace whose final target answer is always the gold normalized answer.

C.9 Role of TRACE in the ARCHER Pipeline

Within ARCHER, TRACE is responsible for converting legacy rationale supervision into the executable action format that HiGRA later refines. This separation is important because TRACE defines the control interface, while HiGRA optimizes how reliably the trained policy uses that interface during executed rollouts. TRACE and HiGRA operate at different stages of the pipeline. TRACE is the compilation and supervised imitation layer; it converts raw dataset rationales into executable structured supervision and uses them to initialize the student policy. HiGRA is the reinforcement refinement layer; it optimizes the SFT-initialized policy using grouped and gated trajectory-level rewards.

In this analogy, TRACE provides the student with a structured reasoning language and explicit tool-use behavior. HiGRA then improves the quality of that behavior by optimizing for correctness, faithful tool use, process discipline, and trace compatibility without requiring a flat and unstable reward over many fine-grained labels.

Appendix D ARCHER Evaluation Metrics

This appendix defines the metrics used to evaluate ARCHER as an executable reasoning policy rather than as a free-form text generator. Let τ=(s1,…,sT)\tau=(s_{1},\dots,s_{T}) denote a model-generated trajectory and let τ⋆=(s1⋆,…,sT⋆⋆)\tau^{\star}=(s_{1}^{\star},\dots,s_{T^{\star}}^{\star}) denote the gold compiled TRACE trajectory. Each state contains an action type, an optional action payload, and an optional tool observation. The predicted answer extracted from τ\tau is denoted by y^\hat{y}, and the gold answer is denoted by y⋆y^{\star}. Accuracy and Valid Trace are reported as percentages. Tool Score, Process Score, tool precision, tool recall, observation consistency, and normalized edit distances are reported on [0,1][0,1] unless stated otherwise.

D.1 Final-Answer Accuracy

Final-answer accuracy measures whether the extracted prediction matches the gold answer after normalization:

Acc=1|𝒟|∑(x,y⋆)∈𝒟𝟏[y^=y⋆].\mathrm{Acc}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(x,y^{\star})\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}=y^{\star}]. (D.1)

For TRACE and HiGRA, y^\hat{y} is extracted from the terminal ANSWER action. If no valid ANSWER action is present, the trajectory is counted as incorrect.

D.2 Valid Trace Rate

Valid Trace is a binary diagnostic, distinct from the fractional format score used inside Process Score. A trajectory is valid when every applicable structural check passes and a final-answer action is present:

V(τ)=𝟏[pfmt(τ)=1] 1[pfinal(τ)=1].V(\tau)=\mathbf{1}[p_{\mathrm{fmt}}(\tau)=1]\,\mathbf{1}[p_{\mathrm{final}}(\tau)=1]. (D.2)

Verification presence, trajectory length, and premature termination remain separate diagnostics and are not folded into V⁡(τ)V(\tau). The reported valid trace rate is

ValidTrace⁡(D)=100|D|​∑τ∈DV⁡(τ).\mathrm{ValidTrace}(D)=\frac{100}{|D|}\sum_{\tau\in D}V(\tau). (D.3)

D.3 Normalized Levenshtein Trace Distance

To measure structural alignment with the compiled executable trace, we compute normalized Levenshtein edit distance over action sequences. Let A⁡(τ)A(\tau) denote the action-type sequence extracted from τ\tau:

A⁡(τ)=(a1,a2,…,aT).A(\tau)=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{T}).

The action-level normalized edit distance is

NEDact​(τ,τ⋆)=Lev⁡(A⁡(τ),A⁡(τ⋆))max⁡(|A⁡(τ)|,|A⁡(τ⋆)|,1),\mathrm{NED}_{\mathrm{act}}(\tau,\tau^{\star})=\frac{\mathrm{Lev}(A(\tau),A(\tau^{\star}))}{\max(|A(\tau)|,|A(\tau^{\star})|,1)}, (D.4)

where Lev⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{Lev}(\cdot,\cdot) is Levenshtein distance.

We also compute an operation-level distance over the sequence of arithmetic operations. Let O⁡(τ)O(\tau) denote the sequence of calculator operation types extracted from the generated trajectory, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. The operation-level normalized edit distance is

NEDop​(τ,τ⋆)=Lev⁡(O⁡(τ),O⁡(τ⋆))max⁡(|O⁡(τ)|,|O⁡(τ⋆)|,1).\mathrm{NED}_{\mathrm{op}}(\tau,\tau^{\star})=\frac{\mathrm{Lev}(O(\tau),O(\tau^{\star}))}{\max(|O(\tau)|,|O(\tau^{\star})|,1)}. (D.5)

Lower values indicate stronger alignment with the compiled executable reasoning structure.

D.4 Tool-Use Precision, Recall, and Observation Consistency

Let C⁡(τ)C(\tau) be the set of tool calls emitted in a generated trajectory and let C⋆​(τ⋆)C^{\star}(\tau^{\star}) be the set of required tool calls in the gold compiled trace. Let match⁡(c,c⋆)\mathrm{match}(c,c^{\star}) indicate that a generated call cc matches a required gold call c⋆c^{\star} in relevant quantities, operation type, and trajectory position.

Tool precision measures whether emitted tool calls are appropriate:

Mprec(c,τ⋆)=[\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{prec}}(c,\tau^{\star})=\mathbf{1}\!\big[ ∃c⋆∈C⋆​(τ⋆):\displaystyle\exists c^{\star}\in C^{\star}(\tau^{\star}): (D.6)
match(c,c⋆)].\displaystyle\mathrm{match}(c,c^{\star})\big].
Prectool=∑c∈C⁡(τ)Mprec​(c,τ⋆)max⁡(|C⁡(τ)|,1).\mathrm{Prec}_{\mathrm{tool}}=\frac{\sum_{c\in C(\tau)}M_{\mathrm{prec}}(c,\tau^{\star})}{\max\!\left(|C(\tau)|,1\right)}. (D.7)

Tool recall measures whether required calls are actually made:

Mrec(c⋆,τ)=[∃c∈C(τ):match(c,c⋆)].M_{\mathrm{rec}}(c^{\star},\tau)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\exists c\in C(\tau):\mathrm{match}(c,c^{\star})\right]. (D.8)
Rectool=∑c⋆∈C⋆​(τ⋆)Mrec​(c⋆,τ)max⁡(|C⋆​(τ⋆)|,1).\mathrm{Rec}_{\mathrm{tool}}=\frac{\sum_{c^{\star}\in C^{\star}(\tau^{\star})}M_{\mathrm{rec}}(c^{\star},\tau)}{\max\!\left(|C^{\star}(\tau^{\star})|,1\right)}. (D.9)

Observation consistency measures whether recorded tool observations agree with executable calculator results. For the ii-th generated tool call, let eie_{i} be the submitted expression and oio_{i} be the recorded observation. The calculator output is fcalc​(ei)f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{i}). We define

ObsCons=∑i=1|C⁡(τ)|𝟏[oi=fcalc(ei)]max⁡(|C⁡(τ)|,1).\mathrm{ObsCons}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{|C(\tau)|}\mathbf{1}[o_{i}=f_{\mathrm{calc}}(e_{i})]}{\max(|C(\tau)|,1)}. (D.10)

D.5 Position of First Error

To analyze where trajectories fail, we identify the earliest causally relevant error in the generated reasoning process. Let Et​(τ)E_{t}(\tau) be an indicator that step tt is the first step where the trajectory becomes incorrect or unreliable. This can include an incorrect decomposition, missing tool call, wrong tool input, inconsistent observation, premature final answer, or malformed trace transition. The first error step is

terr​(τ)=min⁡{t:Et​(τ)=1}.t_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau)=\min\{t:E_{t}(\tau)=1\}. (D.11)

If no error is identified, we set terr​(τ)=∅t_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau)=\varnothing and report the trajectory as a no-error case.

For erroneous trajectories, the normalized first-error position is

PFE⁡(τ)=terr​(τ)T,terr​(τ)≠∅.\mathrm{PFE}(\tau)=\frac{t_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau)}{T},\qquad t_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau)\neq\varnothing. (D.12)

Higher values indicate that the trajectory remains correct for a larger fraction of the reasoning process before failing.

We also group first errors into phases:

ϕerr(τ)∈{\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{err}}(\tau)\in\{ Plan,Tool,Observe,\displaystyle\textsc{Plan},\ \textsc{Tool},\ \textsc{Observe}, (D.13)
Verify,Answer,None}.\displaystyle\textsc{Verify},\ \textsc{Answer},\ \textsc{None}\}.

D.6 Reward-Family Scores

HiGRA defines four macro-reward families:

Rout,Rtool,Rproc,Ralign.R_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{tool}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{proc}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{align}}.

The full training reward is defined in Eq. 1. For reporting in the main tables, we use a diagnostic HiGRA score that summarizes the three most directly comparable reward components:

SHiGRA​(τ)\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}(\tau) =2​Rout​(τ)+Rtool​(τ)\displaystyle=2R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)+R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau) (D.14)
+0.5​Rproc​(τ).\displaystyle+0.5R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau).

This reported score excludes trace alignment and the loop penalty so that it can be compared consistently across the base model, TRACE, and HiGRA. The full HiGRA training reward still includes alignment and loop penalties as described in Section A.

For a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the average diagnostic score is

S¯HiGRA=1|𝒟|​∑τ∈𝒟SHiGRA​(τ).\overline{S}_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}}S_{\mathrm{HiGRA}}(\tau). (D.15)

D.7 Reward-Family Contribution

For each reward family k∈{out,tool,proc,align}k\in\{\mathrm{out},\mathrm{tool},\mathrm{proc},\mathrm{align}\}, we define its weighted contribution over a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} as

Contribk=∑τ∈𝒟wk​Rk​(τ)Z+ε,\mathrm{Contrib}_{k}=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}}w_{k}R_{k}(\tau)}{Z+\varepsilon}, (D.16)

where

Z\displaystyle Z =∑τ∈𝒟(wout​Rout​(τ)+wtool​Rtool​(τ)CLOSE\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}}\Big(w_{\mathrm{out}}R_{\mathrm{out}}(\tau)+w_{\mathrm{tool}}R_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau) (D.17)
OPEN+wproc​Rproc​(τ)+walign​R~align​(τ)).\displaystyle+w_{\mathrm{proc}}R_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau)+w_{\mathrm{align}}\widetilde{R}_{\mathrm{align}}(\tau)\Big).

The constant ε\varepsilon prevents division by zero. For gated rewards, RkR_{k} refers to the gated version when applicable.

D.8 Correlation with Correctness

To test whether a reward family is associated with final-answer correctness, we compute its Pearson correlation with the binary correctness indicator. Let

z(τ)=𝟏[y^=y⋆].z(\tau)=\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}=y^{\star}].

For reward family RkR_{k}, define centered variables

Δ​Rk​(τ)\displaystyle\Delta R_{k}(\tau) =Rk​(τ)−R¯k,\displaystyle=R_{k}(\tau)-\overline{R}_{k}, (D.18)
Δ​z​(τ)\displaystyle\Delta z(\tau) =z⁡(τ)−z¯.\displaystyle=z(\tau)-\overline{z}.

The correlation is

ρk=∑τ∈𝒟Δ​Rk​(τ)​Δ​z​(τ)∑τ∈𝒟Δ​Rk​(τ)2​∑τ∈𝒟Δ​z​(τ)2.\rho_{k}=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}}\Delta R_{k}(\tau)\Delta z(\tau)}{\sqrt{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}}\Delta R_{k}(\tau)^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{D}}\Delta z(\tau)^{2}}}. (D.19)

A higher value indicates that the reward family is more predictive of final-answer correctness.

D.9 AUC of Reward Families

We also compute the area under the ROC curve by treating each reward-family score as a scalar predictor of final-answer correctness. For each reward family RkR_{k}, trajectories are ranked by Rk​(τ)R_{k}(\tau) and evaluated against z⁡(τ)z(\tau). Higher AUC indicates that the reward family better separates correct trajectories from incorrect ones.

Appendix E ARCHER Error Taxonomy and Analysis

This appendix provides the full error taxonomy and annotation protocol used to analyze ARCHER failures in the tool-augmented reasoning setting. The goal of this analysis is twofold. First, we use it for behavior diagnosis, where we identify how and where an executable trajectory fails. Second, we use it for reward auditing, where we check whether the HiGRA reward decomposition assigns credit and blame in a way that agrees with human judgment. Unlike final-answer accuracy, this analysis distinguishes between reasoning failures, tool-use failures, post-tool failures, and structural trace failures.

E.1 Unit of Analysis

Each evaluated example produces a trajectory

τ=(s1,s2,…,sT),\tau=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{T}),

where each state may contain a structured action, an action payload, a tool call, a tool observation, or a final answer. The annotation unit is the full generated trajectory, not only the final answer. For each trajectory, we inspect the input problem, the gold answer, the generated trace, tool calls and observations, the predicted answer, and the corresponding gold compiled trace when available.

A trajectory may contain several mistakes. To avoid over-fragmenting the analysis, each example receives one primary error label and, when useful, one secondary error label. The primary label is assigned to the earliest dominant causal failure. For example, if a model calls the calculator with the wrong expression and then gives an incorrect final answer, the primary label is wrong_tool_input, not merely answer_failure. If a correct tool result is obtained but later misused, the primary label is wrong_after_correct_tool. If the trace is malformed in a way that prevents reliable parsing or execution, the primary label is assigned to the relevant process failure category.

E.2 Sampling Setup

We analyze two complementary GSM-8K test-set samples. The first is an unbiased random sample, used to estimate realistic aggregate error proportions. The second is a diagnostic stratified sample, used to inspect targeted failure types and debug reward behavior. Table E.1 summarizes the two samples.

E.3 Per-Example Analysis Views

For each sampled example, we inspect five complementary views.

Outcome view.

We record the gold answer, predicted answer, and final-answer correctness. We also determine whether the final error is primary or downstream from an earlier reasoning, tool-use, or process failure.

Tool-use view.

We check whether tool use was needed, whether the model attempted a tool call, whether the tool call had a paired observation, whether the observation matches executable output, and whether the final answer correctly uses the tool result.

Process-discipline view.

We inspect whether the generated transcript follows the expected structured format. This includes checking for required tags, malformed action ordering, duplicated or missing actions, premature final answers, excessive verbosity, and non-productive loops.

Trace-alignment view.

We compare the generated trajectory against the compiled gold trace using schema tags, operation tags, calculator-call structure, and verify-step compatibility. This view is used as a soft diagnostic signal rather than as a strict correctness requirement.

Reward-audit view.

We compare the human primary error label with the HiGRA reward decomposition. This allows us to identify whether the dominant automatic penalty agrees with the main human-identified failure.

E.4 Expanded Error Taxonomy

Tables E.2 and E.3 give the full diagnostic taxonomy. These labels are used during manual inspection before being collapsed into the top-level reporting buckets in Table E.5.

E.5 Manual Annotation Schema

Table E.4 shows the annotation schema used for each inspected example. The primary and secondary labels use the taxonomy in Tables E.2 and E.3. The auxiliary fields are used to support reward auditing and qualitative analysis.

E.6 Collapsed Reporting Buckets

For aggregate reporting, we collapse the detailed labels into a smaller set of top-level error buckets. This makes comparisons across model variants easier while retaining the distinctions most relevant to tool-augmented reasoning. Table E.5 defines the reporting buckets.

E.7 Reward-Audit Protocol

For each trajectory, we compute the four HiGRA macro-reward families:

Rout,Rtool,Rproc,Ralign.R_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{tool}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{proc}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{align}}.

We then compare the human primary error label with the dominant automatic reward penalty. Agreement means that the reward family receiving the largest meaningful penalty corresponds to the human-identified failure type. For example, if the human label is wrong_tool_input, the reward audit agrees when the tool-grounding reward is the dominant degraded component. If the human label is format_or_trace_error, the reward audit agrees when the process-discipline or trace-alignment reward accounts for the main penalty.

Table E.6 shows the expected relationship between error labels and HiGRA reward families.

The audit is useful because outcome accuracy alone cannot identify whether a wrong answer came from poor decomposition, missing tool use, incorrect tool input, misuse of a correct observation, or malformed trace structure. HiGRA is intended to preserve this diagnostic information while avoiding direct optimization over a large set of unstable micro-rewards.

E.8 Analysis Workflow

The full workflow consists of five steps. First, we run each model variant on the evaluation set and store the generated trace, tool calls, tool observations, and final answer. Second, we compute automatic outcome correctness, tool-use metadata, process-validity indicators, and HiGRA macro-reward scores. Third, we construct the random and stratified samples described in Table E.1. Fourth, we manually annotate each sampled trajectory using the schema in Table E.4. Fifth, we compare the manual labels against automatic buckets and reward-family decompositions to identify agreement and disagreement cases.

Disagreement cases are especially important. They reveal situations where the automatic reward may over-penalize a secondary issue, under-penalize a causal error, or fail to separate tool input construction from downstream answer synthesis. These cases are used to revise reward weights, gating thresholds, and process penalties.

E.9 Interpretation

For ARCHER, the central question is not only whether the final answer improves, but whether failures become later, more localized, and more attributable to specific executable actions. The taxonomy supports the paper’s main claim that TRACE and HiGRA play complementary roles. TRACE improves observability and structure by converting free-form rationales into executable traces. This makes model failures more inspectable, even when the model is still wrong. HiGRA then improves the quality of those structured trajectories by reducing tool-use errors, stabilizing process behavior, and aligning optimization with the behaviors that make final answers reliable.

Thus, the observed accuracy improvements are not merely answer-level gains. They are accompanied by a shift in the internal failure structure of the model: fewer broad reasoning failures, fewer ungrounded tool interactions, fewer malformed traces, and more trajectories that terminate with verified tool-grounded answers.

Appendix F Computing Infrastructure

All training, reinforcement-learning, inference, and evaluation experiments were run locally on a single Apple MacBook Pro equipped with an Apple M5 Pro system-on-chip, including its integrated CPU and GPU, and 64 GB of unified memory. The machine ran macOS 26.5. GPU acceleration was provided through Apple MLX 0.31.2 and the PyTorch Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend using PyTorch. The remaining software environment used Python 3.10.20. No discrete GPUs or external compute clusters were used.

Appendix G Implementation Details

This appendix summarizes the ARCHER implementation settings.

Randomness.

The default random seed is 42.

G.1 Benchmark Splits and Evaluation Sets

Table G.11 summarizes the dataset sizes and splits used in our experiments. ARCHER uses only the official GSM-8K training split for TRACE and HiGRA training. All remaining benchmarks are used exclusively for evaluation. We preserve the official dataset splits when available and evaluate complete original challenge sets when no separate test split is defined. We do not construct custom splits, subsample evaluation sets, or train on any evaluation benchmark.

MMLU-Math composition.

MMLU-Math consists of the official test partitions for abstract_algebra (100 examples), college_mathematics (100), elementary_mathematics (378), high_school_mathematics (270), and high_school_statistics (216), for a total of 1,064 evaluation examples.

PolyMATH composition.

PolyMATH contains 125 parallel problems at each of four difficulty levels in each of 18 languages, yielding 125×4×18=9,000125\times 4\times 18=9{,}000 evaluated language-problem instances.
